episodes.180526: Showers and thunderstorms developed in a warm and humid airmass over central Pennsylvania with moderate CAPE and very little CIN ahead of an approaching cold front. A few of the storms produced sporadic wind damage, and the widespread nature of this activity allowed the event to evolve into a flash flooding threat as well.
episodes.180529: Widespread showers and thunderstorms brought heavy rain to northern and central New Jersey on the afternoon and evening of July 9.  Rainfall totals were as high as 3 to around 5 inches.
episodes.180742: Thunderstorms moving offshore produced strong wind gusts at Cape Canaveral.
episodes.181287: A thunderstorm briefly became severe as it tracked across eastern portions of Custer County. Quarter sized hail was reported north of Fairburn.
episodes.181600: A sharp upper level disturbance helped spawn slow moving showers and thunderstorms southeast of Lake Ontario over Oswego county. Very heavy rain was centered over central portions of Ontario County. There were numerous reports of closed roads. The highest rainfall reports received were 4.54 inches near Palermo and Phoenix with 3.54 inches near Mexico.
episodes.181648: A cold front moving through a moist and unstable air mass generated severe thunderstorms over portions of central Upper Michigan in the late afternoon and evening |of 7/10.
episodes.181721: Moist, unsettled SW steering flow and low-level convergence brought an early start to storms across the Suwannee River Valley. A short-wave trough impulse approached from the west in the afternoon over an unstable airmass, that further enhanced convective growth as storms approached the Atlantic coast. A strengthening low-level jet prevented the east coast sea breeze from moving far inland but did enhance downdraft strength in storms.
episodes.181722: Moist, unsettled SW steering flow and low-level convergence brought an early start to storms across the Suwannee River Valley. A short-wave trough impulse approached from the west in the afternoon over an unstable airmass, that further enhanced convective growth as storms approached the Atlantic coast. A strengthening low-level jet prevented the east coast sea breeze from moving far inland but did enhance downdraft strength in storms.
episodes.181745: A cold front slowly pushed south across Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours on Monday (7/10) causing thunderstorms to develop across the area.  The strongest storms produced quarter size hail and gusty winds to 50 mph.
episodes.181980: A  waterspout was sighted off of Figure Eight Island.
episodes.182029: A weak frontal boundary over North Florida helped to enhance our typically seabreeze thunderstorms activity resulting in numerous strong marine wind gusts.
episodes.182087: A cold front across South Dakota and Minnesota dropped south across Iowa on the evening of July 10th. Environmental parameters were marginal with CAPE around 1000 J/kg and deep layer shear around 20 to 25 knots. Convergence along the front allowed for storms to develop in the late afternoon, moving across northern and northwest Iowa. Storms strengthened to severe criteria across Emmet county, where hail up to baseball sized was reported along with a wind gust of 58 mph at the Estherville ASOS.
episodes.182143: Multiple rounds of heavy rainfall affected Vermont from late afternoon of the 9th through the early morning hours on the 11th.  During the roughly 36-hour period, 4 to as much as 9 inches of rain fell across much of the Green Mountains, leading to devastating flash and riverine flooding.||Major river flooding was observed in the Winooski, Lamoille and Otter Creek basins with moderate to major flooding in the White River basin. Severe river flooding occurred in the communities of Montpelier, Waterbury, Johnson, Cambridge and Woodstock.  State estimated damage between July 7- July 21 was in the $400-500. Million range between flash flooding and the devastating major river flooding.
episodes.182250: Saturday, July 8th through Monday, July 10th was an active weather period with numerous rounds of heavy rainfall moving across the state.  Thunderstorms developed during the afternoon of Saturday, July 8th with scattered thunderstorms from the White Mountains down through the Monadnocks.  Storms came to an end during the evening hours. Localized 3-hr rainfall totals ranged from 1 to 3���, but no flooding was reported.  ||There was a short break in rainfall activity the night of July 8th through noon on July 9th, before a cluster of showers and thunderstorms developed around noon on Sunday across Cheshire County.  The storms continued to train over the same region with storms repeatedly hitting the same areas in Cheshire County.  Thunderstorms and showers expanded in aerial coverage across western New Hampshire through the late evening.  The rain ended in the hardest hit areas of Cheshire County by 9 PM on July 9th.  ||After a brief lull in the rainfall activity around midnight, rainfall activity began to increase once again during the early morning hours of July 10th.  A large area of rainfall pushed into Western New Hampshire as an area of low pressure moved into Northern New England.  Rainfall was light with areas of moderate rainfall rates through the morning hours of July 10th. Overall rainfall rates were not as heavy as previous days but the rain was more widespread and constant across the Connecticut River Valley region of New Hampshire.  There was a short lull in rainfall across Southwest New Hampshire during the afternoon hours, before a heavy band of heavy rain showers with intense rainfall rates pushed through the region during the evening of July 10th.  Rainfall rates up 1 to 1.25��� per/hour were reported with this band.  Additional flooding was reported as saturated soils led to rapid run-off, especially in Sullivan and Northern Cheshire County.
episodes.182421: Semi-discrete to clustered storms developed along a surface trough in the mid-afternoon in southern South Dakota and northeast Nebraska. Initial updrafts produced large hail with a 2-inch hail stone reported near Niobrara. Strong wind gusts developed later causing widespread tree damage and destroyed a church steeple in Wausa. The strongest measured wind gust was 63 mph near Magnet.
episodes.182512: Multiple rounds of heavy rainfall affected portions of northeastern New York from late afternoon of the 9th through the early morning hours on the 11th. During the roughly 36-hour period, two to as much as five inches of rain affected these counties in several bursts. This led to scattered areas of flash flooding, some significant to severe.
episodes.182531: Widespread showers and thunderstorms with heavy rainfall affected the region on July 10, 2023 leading to areas of significant to severe flash flooding.
episodes.182553: Scattered thunderstorms impacted central and southwestern Montana. The strongest storms developed over Great Falls which had wind gusts around 50 mph, and the Canyon Ferry Lake area where gusts up to 63 mph were officially recorded. Other storms across the area generally produced wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph and small hail.
episodes.182620: Two rounds of storms were seen late on the 9th ahead of a cold front dropping out of Canada. The first round developed during the evening hours across the Brainerd Lakes region following an afternoon of very warm and humid conditions. These storms quickly become strong but a lack of shear led to them quickly falling apart. A few storms were able to produce hail to the size of golf balls before weakening. Later in the evening storms developed across northern Minnesota ahead of the cold front and moved into the Iron Range region. These storms were mainly sub-severe, but a few did produce isolated damaging wind gusts leading to a few downed trees and branches.
episodes.182621: Storms developed ahead of a cold front moving across northwest Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours on the 10th. Most of the storms remained below severe limits, but one storm over Price County was able to produce 1 inch hail before moving out of the region.
episodes.182730: Severe Thunderstorms passed through northwestern Minnesota, producing large hailstones. The largest hailstone out of these storms was 2 inches.
episodes.182786: Some high-based thunderstorms across the western portions of the Billings Forecast Area produced some severe wind gusts.
episodes.182898: A shortwave trough moving into the southern Great Plains resulted in afternoon thunderstorms. A few thunderstorms became strong to severe, producing localized severe wind gusts.
episodes.182951: There was significant flash flooding including a building collapse and a water rescue in Canandaigua in the late afternoon as some estimates point to a 100 year flood event. A state of emergency was declared for Ontario county. Flash flooding also occurred in portions of Lewis County into the early evening. Numerous roads in these counties were flooded and impassable with some washed out. A weak wave of low pressure stalled along a trough combined with increasing moisture and instability to focus waves of showers and thunderstorms with very heavy rain. The axis of heaviest rain stretched from Ontario County to Lewis County. Rainfall amounts along this axis were uneven, but there were pockets of extreme rainfall with over 5.5 inches near Canandaigua in Ontario county and over 4 inches between Lowville and Croghan in Lewis county.
episodes.182987: An anomalously amplified mid level trough moving east from the Great Lakes closed off and brought widespread showers and scattered thunderstorms which lead to flooding in western and central Massachusetts. Many roads were closed and cars were stuck in flood waters.
episodes.182988: An anomalously amplified mid level trough moving east from the Great Lakes closed off and brought widespread showers and scattered thunderstorms which lead to flooding in Rhode Island.  Many roads were closed and cars were stuck in flood waters.
episodes.182997: A typical summer pattern persisted with scattered thunderstorms across the area with a few reports of severe weather.
episodes.183006: A typical summer pattern prevailed with scattered thunderstorms producing occasional gusty winds across the coastal waters.
episodes.183017: A strong upper-level system brought widespread rounds of showers and thunderstorms to eastern New York on July 9-11, 2023. The steadiest and heaviest rainfall occurred during the afternoon hours on July 9, the early morning hours on July 10 and during the evening hours on July 10 into the overnight hours on July 11. Rainfall totals varied greatly from region to region but the hardest hit areas (Hudson Valley and into northeastern Hamilton County) received 3 to 6 inches of rainfall.||Areal and flash flooding was primarily focused across areas along the Hudson River on July 9-10. Damage consisted of closed and washed out roads. A section of Metro-North's railroad tracks were washed out due to flood waters from Poughkeepsie southward.||The combination of heavy rain and beaver dam failures resulted in destruction of roads, bridges and sidewalks across northeastern Hamilton County during the early morning hours on July 11 focused on the areas of Long Lake and Blue Mountain Lake. A State of Emergency was declared for the towns of Long Lake and Indian Lake. New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State of Emergency for Hamilton County. Hamilton County Emergency Manager estimated damage to be in the millions of dollars.||In addition to the heavy rainfall, a few severe thunderstorms also developed across portions of the Hudson Valley leading to downed trees and wires. A lightning strike caused an auto body shop to catch fire.
episodes.183018: A strong upper-level system brought widespread rounds of showers and embedded thunderstorms to southern Vermont on July 9-11, 2023. The steadiest and heaviest rainfall occurred from the afternoon hours on July 9 through the morning hours on July 10. Rainfall totals generally ranged between 2.50 and 5.00 inches with some localized amounts of around 6 inches across the southern Green Mountains.||This rainfall resulted in areas of areal and flash flooding. The hardest hit area was in the Town of Londonderry as water flooded numerous roads and caused portions of the area to be inaccessible. Many other roadways across southern Vermont were closed due to flooding from the combination of heavy rainfall and rivers overflowing their banks. A few water rescues were also conducted to assist those in rising flood waters.||Vermont Governor Phil Scott declared a state of emergency on July 10 as a result of the flooding. President Joe Biden later approved a major disaster declaration for the state of Vermont.
episodes.183019: A strong upper-level system brought widespread rounds of showers and thunderstorms to western Massachusetts on July 9-10, 2023. The steadiest and heaviest rainfall occurred during the early morning hours on July 10 which resulted in areas of flooding. Rainfall totals were generally in the 1.50 to 4.00 inch range.||Areas receiving flooding included the City of North Adams and the towns of Clarksburg, Becket, Sheffield, Washington and Great Barrington mainly consisting of closed and/or washed out roads and flooded homes/basements. Damage within the City of North Adams was estimated at $1.5 million. A State of Emergency was issued for North Adams, Becket, Hinsdale and Clarksburg due to the flooding.
episodes.183020: A strong upper-level system brought widespread rounds of showers and thunderstorms to northwestern Connecticut on July 9-10, 2023. Northern and western portions of the county were hardest hit with rainfall amounts between 4 and 7 inches. This resulted in numerous reports of flash flooding and washed out roads and culverts.||A local declaration of emergency was issued in the Town of Norfolk following flash flood damage along Route 272. The damage along this road caused some homes to become isolated. A State of Emergency was also issued by Goshen First Selectman Todd Carusillo.
episodes.183094: Isolated showers and thunderstorms developed across parts of SE PA on July 10th with a few thunderstorms turning severe, producing damaging wind gusts.
episodes.183136: Strong thunderstorms dropped large hail in the Marquette area during the late afternoon and evening of the 10th.
episodes.183259: Supercells developed in the central Sandhills during the afternoon of July 10 and drifted south into southwest Nebraska through the early evening hours. Multiple reports of large, some significantly severe, hail and damaging winds were received.
episodes.183309: A slow moving thunderstorm produced flooding and a landspout near Lebleu Settlement.
episodes.183310: Thunderstorms moved across the marine area and produced high winds.
episodes.183311: Thunderstorms moved across the marine area and produced high winds.
episodes.183355: Rain during the morning of July 9th helped to saturate the ground, and additional thunderstorms in an anomalously high moisture environment during the early evening hours created flash flooding.  Wayne and Shenango Townships in Lawrence County were particularly hard hit, with at least eight homes in these areas impacted by flooding. Many roads were also impacted. An isolated instance of wind damage was also noted in Beaver County.
episodes.183411: Typical summertime thunderstorms produced some minor wind damage, localized flooding, and two injuries due to lightning.
episodes.183435: Weak low pressure systems embedded in a hot and humid airmass over the region contributed to several rounds of heavy rain-producing thunderstorm activity. Isolated locations in Central New York received between 2 to 4 inches of rainfall and experienced flooding of streams, creeks and roadways.
episodes.183544: During the late afternoon a strong thunderstorm produced hail up to nickel size near Burlington.
episodes.183546: Strong to severe thunderstorms moved south through Southern Nebraska into Northwest Kansas during the late afternoon during the late afternoon and early evening.  Thunderstorm winds were strong enough to break off a six inch diameter tree limb in Benkelman.  The largest hail reported was near Trenton.
episodes.183547: During the late afternoon into early evening scattered thunderstorms moved across Northwest Kansas.  The strongest thunderstorm produced wind gusts up to 68 MPH near Ludell.  Further west two colliding boundaries produced a short-lived landspout tornado north of Weskan.  The largest hail for the day was reported north of Colby.
episodes.183593: A stalled frontal boundary remained over the area which produced multiple rounds of torrential rainfall form heavy thunderstorms from July 9th through July 10th. CAPE values of 2500 to 3500 J/kg and PWAT values of near 1.8 allowed heavy thunderstorm development to produce rainfall rates of 2-3 inches per hour at times. There were parts of the area that receive anywhere from 3-5 inches of rain in a several hour period with some spots seeing upwards of 8 inches. This allowed for the issuance of a localized Flash Flood Emergency for portion of the Lower Hudson Valley.
episodes.183594: A stalled frontal boundary remained over the area which produced multiple rounds of torrential rainfall form heavy thunderstorms from July 9th through July 10th. CAPE values of 2500 to 3500 J/kg and PWAT values of near 1.8 allowed heavy thunderstorm development to produce rainfall rates of 2-3 inches per hour at times. There were parts of the area that receive anywhere from 3-5 inches of rain in a several hour period.
episodes.183634: A line of thunderstorms moved off the Georgia coast in the early afternoon hours and produced strong wind gusts across the nearby coastal waters.
episodes.183723: Late afternoon thunderstorms developed in the exit region of a strong jet streak in northwest flow aloft, focused along a prefrontal trough across southeast South Dakota. Storms quickly became severe, with MLCAPE of up to 1500 J/kg and deep layer shear around 40 knots.
episodes.183726: Late afternoon thunderstorms developed in the exit region of a strong jet streak in northwest flow aloft, focused along a prefrontal trough as it moved from southeast South Dakota into northwest Iowa. Storms quickly became severe, with MLCAPE of up to 1500 J/kg and deep layer shear around 40 knots.
episodes.184013: Multiple thunderstorms developed along a stalled frontal boundary as an upper level trough approached the area. Some of these thunderstorms were severe and produced damaging wind gusts.
episodes.184066: A typical summertime diurnal convective pattern was in place. In the early morning, convection remained in the marine areas while convection triggered closer to land during the afternoon.
episodes.184127: A line of thunderstorms that were associated with a southward advancing cold front proceeded across Central and Southern MN and Western WI. The meteorological setup was considered a High CAPE/Low Shear environment. Or in other words, plenty of available energy for storms to develop, but lack of turning winds with height to support rotating updrafts. Therefore, large hail was the primary threat with the line of storms that developed from Cumberland, WI down to Redwood Falls, MN and farther south.||These strong storms produced 50 kt wind gusts which snapped a 10-inch diameter tree 8 miles NNE of Menomonie, WI (Dunn) and large hail. Measured hail sizes from these storms ranged from nickel size to golf ball size hail with most falling as quarter size. A few of the highest hailstones measured: |1.75 inches - Golf Ball - 4 miles N of Holcombe, WI (Chippewa)|1.50 inches - Ping Pong Ball - 5 miles E of Hudson, WI (St. Croix)|1.25 inches - Half-Dollar - 7 miles SW of Ladysmith, WI (Rusk).
episodes.184171: A few thunderstorms developed during the evening of July 09th. One of the storms produced large hail across far northern Morrison county.
episodes.184350: A strong system moved through Eastern Washington and brought scattered thunderstorms. The main areas stretched along Highway 2 from Waterville Plateau to Northern Spokane County.
episodes.184354: Isolated thunderstorm associated with a surface trough of low pressure produced a funnel cloud across portions of northeast North Carolina.
episodes.185954: A shortwave riding along a frontal boundary produced heavy rainfall over north Georgia on the morning of July 10. Rainfall amounts of 2 to 4 inches were common over northwest Georgia, with portions of Floyd county receiving above 4 inches. Although convective activity diminished into the pre-dawn hours as this system moved southward into Atlanta, it was not before flash flooding was reported in the city of Rome.

Three to five inches of rain fell in southwest Lawrence over a 3 hour period.  At least eight homes were impacted by flooding in Wayne and Shenango Townships. Numerous roads were closed in the area and several water rescues from houses and cars were performed by local firefighters. The most significant damage in Shenango Township occurred around Union Valley, Snake Run, and Lower Boyd School Roads, the latter of which was undermined, creating damage to the asphalt. Roads impacted in Wayne Township included Shenango Stop, Union Valley, Snake Run, Chewton-West Pittsburg, Fletcher Hill, Boyd School, Lower Boyd School, Old Pittsburgh, and Union Valley Roads. McKee Run was reported to overflow its banks.||The Lawrence County Commissioners issued a disaster declaration for the entire county, with the Shenango and Wayne Township supervisors adopting similar measures for their respective municipalities.
Minor flooding occurred along the Neshanic River in Raritan Township.

Two to four inches of rain fell during the evening hours on July 9. This led to areas of significant flash flooding, most notably in the towns of Saranac, Redford and Altona. The town of Altona was hardest hit, with numerous road washouts.
Lay Lake Fire Department reported McGowans Ferry Road flooded and impassable near County Road 33.
Quarter to Ping-Pong ball sized hail reported by public east of Borup. Time estimated via radar.
Deveines Road is closed due to flash flooding.

Radar estimates of 2 to 4 inches of rain fell across the affected area leading to a few areas of flash flooding, most notably in the Bloomfield, VT area on Patnaude Rd.

The Emergency Manager reported a home flooded along the 300 block of Greenwood Avenue due to floodwaters from an overwhelmed storm drain. Radar estimates indicate that between 3.5 and 4.5 inches of rain occurred over the area, resulting in the flash flooding.
DOT reports debris and flooding on Taconic State parkway northbound at Yorktown. All lanes blocked.
Vermont Route 30 was closed near West Hill Road South in Jamaica due to a washout and flooding.

The Emergency Manager reported numerous reports of flooding within the city of Rome. Several buildings experienced flooding, including six feet of water in the first floor of Kindred Hospital on Turner McCall Blvd. Additionally, numerous other roads were closed with water two to three feet deep. There was one report of a rescue from a stalled vehicle. Radar estimates indicate between 3.5 and 4.5 inches occurred over the area, resulting in the flash flooding.

The Emergency Manager reported flooding along Calhoun Road, north of Model High School, and of Ward Mountain Road. Both of the roadways were flooded due to high water from Dozier Creek. Radar estimates indicate that between 3.5 and 4.5 inches occurred over the area, resulting in high runoff rates and quickly rising creeks and tributaries.

Training showers and thunderstorms with heavy rainfall affected this area between the early morning and early to mid afternoon on July 10. Observations and radar estimates show 3 to 7 inches of rainfall occurred, with localized totals to 8 inches. Severe to devastating flash flooding occurred in several towns during this period, most notably in Weston, Ludlow, Plymouth and Bridgewater.
Vermont Route 30 in Winhall near Stoney Hill Road was closed due to flooding.

All lanes flooded on Taconic State Parkway near Tompkins Corners.
The Taconic State Parkway was flooded at the Beekman Road Ramp.
Heavy rain during the afternoon of the 9th caused overnight flooding of the Great Brook in Langdon. The Brook flooded Old Stage Road.

A portion of Weatogue Road near Bartholomew's Cobble Reservation was washed out due to heavy rainfall in the Town of Sheffield. In addition, a section of Rannapo Road was close closed due to water over the road up to 1.5 feet deep.
State Route 343 was closed in both directions at Old Route 22 due to flooding in Dover Plains.
Emans Road at State Route 82 was flooded due to heavy rainfall.
Route 32 was closed between Tibbits Avenue and Bridge Avenue due to flooding.
Various roads in the Town of Great Barrington were closed due to flooding. The worst flooding occurred along Route 41 near Welcome Street.

The combination of heavy rainfall and the West River rising over its banks has led to flash flooding around the Town of Londonderry. Parts of town were evacuated and many of its highways (Vermont Routes 11 and 100) and local roads were impassable.
A section of Route 63 in Falls Village from Cobble Road to Barnes Road was closed due to flooding.
Two houses were evacuated along Preston Mountain Road due to rising flood waters.
Multiple Roads were closed along the US Route 7 corridor as well as Schaghticoke Road from floodwaters caused by the swollen Housatonic River in the Town of Kent.
The Taconic State Parkway was flooded at the Beekman Road Ramp.

Observations and radar estimates show 1.5 to 4 inches of rain fell in the area with scattered reports of flash flooding, most notably in the towns of Barton and Orleans.
Flooding was reported in the Town of Washington including along Route 8 at the Town Park and on Frost Road near Washington Mountain Road.
Benton Hill Road was closed due to a wash out in the Town of Becket.

Training showers and thunderstorms with heavy to torrential rainfall affected this area from the early morning to early afternoon hours on July 10, 2023. Observations and radar estimates show 3 to 6 inches of rain occurred, with localized amount to 7-8 inches. This lead to areas of significant flash flooding with numerous roads closed. The towns of Berlin, Williamstown, Roxbury and Middlesex were most impacted, with scattered reports elsewhere.

The Cold River came out of banks on the evening of the 10th following heavy rains. The river had been running high due to multiple rounds of heavy rain over the previous few days. After approximately 1 to 3 inches of additional rain that afternoon, the river spiked to the second highest level on record at the Alstead USGS river gage (period of record 2010-2023). The river crested at 11.67 feet, with a discharge of 10,300 cfs. The flow recorded has an annual exceedance probability between 1% and 0.2% levels.  The high flowing water came out of banks along Route-123A in South Acworth and Acworth Road in Alstead. Acworth Fire Chief rescued 12 people from their homes on Route 123A. He said several cars were swept by water but there were no injuries in those incidents. The floodwaters caused damage to the southbound lane on Acworth Road. In Lempster South Road and River Road were flooded.

A severe thunderstorm produced a widespread area of somewhat sporadic straight line wind damage. A survey team found damage beginning in northeast portion of East Rockhill Township, where a tree fell onto a house on East Rock Road. The damaging winds continued in an east to southeast swath into the southwest portion of Bedminster Township. The survey team noted numerous uprooted trees, downed limbs and branches in this area. Several of these fell onto powerlines, causing powerlines and some power poles to fall. There were a couple of snapped trees, however these were weakened by interior rotting of the trunks. There were dozens of corn fields that had leaning or flattened corn stalks in this area as well. As the strong winds continued southeast into Plumstead Township, the damage became noticeably more sporadic and generally less severe in nature. A few more trees were uprooted, some falling onto powerlines. The last large tree that was found uprooted was on Curly Hill Road, where it also downed powerlines and a few power poles.
